items.title: 5 Reasons Why Home Is the Hardest Place to Lead
items.description:
Olympic hurdlers are always interesting to watch. They sprint at top speed, leap over the barriers, and rarely break their stride as they fix their eyes on the finish line. The post 5 Reasons Why Home Is the Hardest Place to Lead appeared first on All Pro Dad.
items.content:
Olympic hurdlers are always interesting to watch. They sprint at top speed, leap over the barriers, and rarely break their stride as they fix their eyes on the finish line. It’s easy to draw a parallel in our careers. We study something, put countless hours into it, and go after defined goals. It’s not always easy, but chasing down success can seem straightforward. But how does this apply to being a leader at home?

If work is similar to Olympic hurdles, life at home can feel more like a muddy obstacle course. There’s no straight line to follow, wild challenges pop up often, and it feels like we’re one misstep away from an injury. Leading at home is hard. On many days, it feels harder than the challenges we face at work. Don’t get discouraged if it feels like you’re failing. It’s hard because it’s important. Here are 5 reasons why home is the hardest place to lead.

1. You can’t fire your children.

If employees are disrespectful, consistently late, or underperforming, you can fire them. If your kids aren’t listening, you don’t just kick them out. You’re a parent forever, no matter what. You must lead with the long-term in mind. Being a leader at home comes with weightier expectations because parenting is a commitment, not a contract. When it’s especially tough because the kids aren’t listening, remember that children are a gift and worth the effort it takes to guide them into maturity.

2. There is no paid or unpaid time off.

Who doesn’t love a nice vacation? The average U.S. worker gets 10–20 paid days off per year. As a husband and father, you’ll get zero. In fact, overtime is required, and you’ll probably work harder on holidays. There are no breaks from leading our homes, but that’s not a bad thing. Our families should get our full attention and effort. Everybody likes breaks. Me-time is good. But, as tough as it is, our families deserve all of us, all the time, physically, emotionally, and mentally.

3. There are no salaries, bonuses, or raises.

Money is a universal motivator. There may be some financial incentive to crushing it at your office, but those bonuses aren’t coming at home. In fact, your family is going to cost a lot of money. Leading at home means providing food, clothing, and more. Don’t get me started on braces. Dads can feel like a walking ATM. It can be frustrating, but fight the urge to stop leading when the payoff isn’t obvious. Embrace those intangible riches like hugs, love notes, and laughs. You become a selfless servant when love is your motivation.

4. There are no awards, accolades, or applause.

If you’re waiting for a pat on the back for assembling those bunk beds or mopping the floor, it may never come. Leading at home requires being internally motivated, knowing there are no trophies for raising successful kids or loving your wife well. It would be great to be recognized for all the hard work you do as a dad or husband, but if you’re only in it for the recognition, then your heart posture is off. Lead at home because your kids need it, and your wife deserves it. Finding satisfaction in knowing you’re putting the needs of your family ahead of your own is the reward.

5. There are daily HR issues.

Parents are constantly trying to hit moving targets. One minute you’re cementing a family budget with your spouse. The next you’re trying not to lose your cool after the kids flushed apples down the toilet. Leadership requires a lot from us, especially when there are so many diverse hoops to jump through in the same day. We have to manage marital conflict, sibling arguments, bullying, sickness, school grades, talking back, crying, lying, and more. There’s an emotional toll to leading.

Sound off: What is the hardest job you’ve ever had?

items.title: Why Couples Fight About Chores (and What to Do Instead)
items.description:
When Nancie and I first got married, she said, “Can you please wash your shaving cream and whiskers out of the sink?” I had never thought about that one day in my life. It’s not a cereal bowl. She wants our bed made up every day, complete with seven pillows we’re just going to take [...]

The post Why Couples Fight About Chores (and What to Do Instead) appeared first on All Pro Dad.
items.content:
When Nancie and I first got married, she said, “Can you please wash your shaving cream and whiskers out of the sink?” I had never thought about that one day in my life. It’s not a cereal bowl. She wants our bed made up every day, complete with seven pillows we’re just going to take back off that night. Makes no sense to me. Makes complete sense to her. I’m not alone. A friend of mine put it differently. His side of the bathroom sink is spotless. Her side, his word, is “nasty.” He said, “And I hate it when her stuff crosses over into my land.”

That’s the thing about arguing about chores: It usually isn’t about the chore at all. Clean to one person is not clean to another. What bothers one person doesn’t bother the other. What one person notices, another person will never see. So before you fight about who’s right, here’s why couples fight about chores (and what to do instead).

If you’re the messy one…

1. Work to really understand your spouse’s definition of clean.

You don’t have to agree with it. You just have to understand it’s real to them, not made up to annoy you. For a lot of us, clean was defined in the house we grew up in, and we’re still operating off that old definition without realizing it. Once you know where your wife’s definition comes from, it stops feeling like a random rule and starts feeling like something you can work with.

2. Stop trying to reason your way out of it.

You’re never going to win that argument, and it’s not worth the cost. “But it’s just a sink” has never once changed anyone’s mind mid-fight. Arguing about chores rarely gets settled with logic anyway; it gets settled with a decision to let it go. The goal isn’t to be right. The goal is her. Being right and being close to her aren’t always the same thing.

3. If logic isn’t going to get you there, do the chore anyway, simply because you love her.

You don’t need a good reason to rinse the sink or make the bed. You need a good reason to love her, and you already have one: You married her. Let that be enough some days, even when the request still doesn’t make sense to you.

4. Remember, most of what she’s asking for takes 60 seconds, five minutes, or 10 minutes.

I would rather build a log cabin than unload the dishwasher, so I make a sport of it, timing myself unloading the dishwasher. I’m great at it. The task usually isn’t the problem. It’s the story I tell myself about the task.

5. Have the conversation when you’re not in the middle of a moment.

Nothing gets resolved while she’s holding your whiskers in a paper towel. Bring it up later, calmly, and maybe with a laugh at yourself first, and you’ll actually hear each other instead of just defending yourselves. Timing changes everything. The same sentence that sounds like an attack at 10 p.m. can sound like a fair ask the next morning.

If you’re the neat spouse married to a messy one:

1. Remember whatever your spouse does well that you can’t, and does without complaint.

Maybe their neatness, or lack of it, isn’t the problem either. Marriage is a trade of strengths, not a scoreboard of chores. The guy who leaves his shaving cream in the sink might also be the guy who never lets a hard conversation go unfinished.

2. Stop keeping score.

Chores might be the clearest place where we keep score in marriage because it’s so easy to measure. A made bed. A clean sink. A dishwasher unloaded. But arguing about chores turns into arguing about worth fast, and once it becomes about who does more, nobody’s actually listening anymore.

3. Let it go as much as you can, or even do more than your fair share.

Not because it’s fair. It’s not. But because serving each other is part of marriage, and somebody has to go first. It might as well be you. That’s not weakness; that’s leadership, and it’s one of the fastest ways to stop arguing about chores before it even starts

4. Ask before you assume.

A messy spouse isn’t automatically a careless one. Before you decide she doesn’t care, ask her what’s actually going on: tiredness, a different priority in the moment, or just genuinely not seeing what you see. You might be surprised how often it’s not about you at all.

5. Say thank you for the effort, not just the result.

If she tries and misses the mark, that still counts for something. Noticing the effort goes a lot further than noticing what’s still wrong. Nobody feels loved by a scorecard; they feel loved by someone who sees them trying.

I grew up with my dad and my brother. We were like bears with furniture. Then I married the neatest woman on the planet, and over the years, I’ve learned to notice. My sink is clean. I make the bed. This bear has learned, and your spouse can too. Promise.

Sound off: What have you done to stop the chore battle in your marriage?

The post Why Couples Fight About Chores (and What to Do Instead) appeared first on All Pro Dad.

items.title: Are We Raising a Generation of Gambling Addicts?
items.description:
Are we raising a generation of gambling addicts? That may sound like an extreme question, but I think it’s one we need to ask. A new study from Common Sense Media found that 36% of boys ages 11 to 17 reported gambling in the past year. That’s more than one in three teen boys. That [...]

The post Are We Raising a Generation of Gambling Addicts? appeared first on All Pro Dad.
items.content:
Are we raising a generation of gambling addicts? That may sound like an extreme question, but I think it’s one we need to ask. A new study from Common Sense Media found that 36% of boys ages 11 to 17 reported gambling in the past year. That’s more than one in three teen boys. That number is closer to 50% for just 17-year-old boys.

When I was growing up, gambling was something I associated with Las Vegas, Atlantic City, or the occasional poker game. I didn’t gamble for the first time until my mid-20s. Our kids are growing up in a very different and more dangerous environment. Gambling is everywhere—at sporting events, on social media, in video games, and other places online. Our kids are getting hooked in ways you might not expect. What can dads do about it? Here are some things every dad needs to know about gambling and teenagers.

Why is gambling becoming a problem for kids?

Gambling doesn’t always look like gambling anymore. Kids see betting odds during sporting events, hear commentators talk about parlays, see gambling advertisements, and encounter gambling-like experiences in video games. Let that sink in. It’s being normalized in the video games they play. They may start seeing gambling as normal entertainment before they’re old enough to understand the risks.

Now, let’s be clear: The 36% statistic doesn’t mean 36% of boys are gambling addicts. It means they reported gambling in the past year. But it does tell us something important: Gambling is already part of the experience of a significant number of boys.

What are the downsides of gambling for kids?

Financial Problems

Kids and teens can develop the mindset that money is something you can win quickly instead of something you earn through work, patience, investments, and wise decisions. When they lose, they may try to win it back, creating a cycle of chasing losses. When I lost $200 gambling, the first thing I wanted to do was win it back. Fortunately, I was in my mid-20s and better able to think through the consequences. Our kids are still developing the capability to do that.

Addiction and Compulsive Behavior

Gambling can become compulsive. A teenager may start thinking about gambling constantly, want to gamble more often, or feel like he needs to keep playing to get the same excitement. Because kids and teenagers are still developing impulse control and decision-making skills, they may be particularly vulnerable to risky behavior.

Anxiety, Depression, and Stress

Gambling problems can bring stress, anxiety, shame, and depression. Imagine a teenager losing money he wasn’t supposed to bet. Now he has to hide it from his parents. Then he loses more trying to win it back. Now he’s lying and worried about being caught. Suddenly, the problem isn’t just money. It’s secrecy, stress, and shame.

School and Relationship Problems

If a teenager is constantly thinking about the next bet or how to recover money he lost, that can take attention away from school, friendships, sports, and other healthy activities. Gambling can also damage trust. Kids may hide what they’re doing, lie about money, or borrow money from friends and family. When gambling becomes more important to teenagers than relationships, the people closest to them get hurt.

Long-Term Risk

Early exposure may establish habits and attitudes that follow kids into adulthood. Again, the 36% number doesn’t mean one in three boys will become addicted. But it should make us ask whether we’re creating a culture where gambling has become so normal that our kids don’t recognize the risks.

What can dads do about teens and gambling?

Start the conversation before there’s a problem.

Don’t wait until you discover your son has placed a bet. Talk about gambling with teenagers before it becomes personal.

Ask questions like:

“What do your friends think about gambling?”
“What do you think about sports gambling?”
“What parts of your video games have gambling? (Example: “Are there parts where you can pay money for something that’s unknown, like a box with mystery treasure in it?”
“What do you think some of the dangers of gambling are?”

The goal isn’t to interrogate your kid. It’s to make sure he knows he can talk to you. Be a safe place. Try to temper your reactions and encourage his responses.

Teach them how gambling works.

Our kids need to understand that gambling companies aren’t in business to lose money. The odds are designed so the house wins over time. Talk about probability, odds, and why a “sure thing” isn’t a sure thing.

I once showed a group of middle school boys how this works using M&M’s and playing cards. I became the house, and they became the players. By the end, the house had taken almost all of the M&M’s. It was a simple way to show them that the house isn’t trying to help you win.

Pay attention to what your kids are doing online.

Know what games they play. Know what apps they use. Know what they’re watching and what their friends are talking about. Gambling doesn’t always look like gambling. Some gaming mechanics involve randomized rewards or purchases that can resemble gambling. Parents need to understand what their kids are being exposed to.

Create an environment where kids can tell the truth.

If your child makes a mistake, you want him to come to you and say, “Dad, I did something stupid.” That doesn’t mean there shouldn’t be consequences. It means your relationship is strong enough that your child doesn’t feel like he has to hide. Our goal isn’t just to keep our kids from making bad decisions. It’s to build the kind of relationship where they come to us when they’re facing a bad decision.

Sound off: Have you talked to teenagers in your home about gambling? What have you said to them about sports betting or gambling online?

*If you have a problem with gambling, there’s no shame. Call 1-800-MY-RESET for help today.

items.title: Benjamin Watson: 6 Ways to Help Your Kids Define Success
items.description:
Boyd Epley was a pole vaulter who was known for his impressive workout regimen. The University of Nebraska took notice and hired him to be their football strength coach. He quickly had the athletes working harder than ever. He changed their weightlifting routine. He updated team conditioning. And when the Huskers won back-to-back national championships [...]

The post Benjamin Watson: 6 Ways to Help Your Kids Define Success appeared first on All Pro Dad.
items.content:
Boyd Epley was a pole vaulter who was known for his impressive workout regimen. The University of Nebraska took notice and hired him to be their football strength coach. He quickly had the athletes working harder than ever. He changed their weightlifting routine. He updated team conditioning. And when the Huskers won back-to-back national championships in 1970 and 1971, the rest of the college football world spotted the reason. Rival coaches flew to Lincoln to copy Nebraska’s new methods.

One motivation tool Epley implemented was the giant leaderboards he hung in the weight room. The signs displayed everyone’s weightlifting records. Each player could look up while lifting and see how far they’d come that season. Their progress was trackable. Those signs reminded the players that their individual success, growth, and future were all up to them. That’s a lesson I want my kids to embrace. If comparison is a big thing in your house, or if you want your kids to have a healthy view of achievement, here are 6 ways to help your kids define success.

1. Remember, there will always be someone “better.”

I showed up eager to run at the NFL Combine right after college. I clocked a 4.57 40-yard dash time, which is pretty fast. A few weeks later, at my Georgia Pro Day, I ran even faster—4.41. That time was incredible for me, but it wouldn’t even crack the all-time top 100 pre-draft times recorded.

Our kids need to know they will likely never be the fastest, smartest, tallest, or any other -est. And that’s OK. Are they becoming the best version of themselves? I was never trying to be Usain Bolt. I wasn’t concerned with being the best, just my best. When being No. 1 is the only acceptable outcome, our kids will struggle with their identity. They’ll feel inadequate when they underachieve and start to believe they’ll never be enough. When others’ success becomes the metric by which we measure our own, we’ll often walk away disappointed. Remind your kids to compare themselves to yesterday, not someone else.

2. There’s no cookie-cutter time frame.

Has your child ever worked hard at something like learning to ride a bike or raise their SAT score? What takes one person six hours may take the next person six months. Both timelines can be defined as successful. It all depends on the person. The problem for our kids is that “fastest” is often equated with “best” or “right,” and that’s simply not true.

Learning how to define success for children starts with acknowledging that there is no cookie-cutter version. When helping kids define success, ask them about their desired timeline. Is it relevant to their goal? Can it be done as quickly as they think? Help them see that not everything happens on schedule. Guide them as they do their best, and encourage them for as long as it takes.

3. You get to define success to children.

Do you know how to define success to children? During my time in the NFL, I saw up close how success got defined differently. In 2007, I caught a career-high six touchdowns. My teammate, Randy Moss, also had a career year—23 touchdowns. The final numbers were very different, but we both had successful seasons because we fulfilled different roles on the same team.

Your kids need to learn that same lesson. Success isn’t about matching someone else’s accomplishments; it’s about making the most of their opportunities and abilities. I wasn’t trying to be Randy Moss. He was one of the greatest receivers ever. I was trying to be the best version of myself. That’s how I defined success.

4. Others shouldn’t dictate your happiness.

If your kids’ attitude spikes or dips based on how other people view them or their accomplishments, they’re in for a rough time. Different peer groups will demand different things from your kids. Those subtle influences will tempt your kid to become a chameleon, doing what it takes to fit in. Chasing others’ approval is exhausting.

Kids will feel the pressure to be athletic, smart, funny, and more. When their happiness is tied to peers’ opinions, that’s a recipe for heartache. Kids will begin to question if the successes they do see are “good enough.” If your child spends his or her life trying to satisfy everyone, they’ll be unhappy more often than not. Remind them that being authentic is the goal.

5. Learning to work hard is the reward.

Ask any NFL player, and they’ll tell you that training camp is hard. It’s long days in the sun and a physical beating. I always just wanted the season to start, but I understood that practice produced discipline, resilience, and sacrifice. All of those things are key variables to success. This applies to more than just football. Your kids may not like all the tedious steps that usually precede success, but there are lessons in the grind.

Your kids won’t see the payoff if they don’t embrace the hard work. Better grades don’t just happen. They require studying. Kids must memorize lines if they want a role in the school play. No matter what their goal is, the hard work to get there, even though it’s sometimes unpleasant, isn’t wasted because it’s building toward something great. They won’t feel the satisfaction of achievement without the grind.

6. Failure often precedes success.

Failure and success are intertwined. If your children expect everything to go according to script, remind them that even the most successful people failed in pursuit of their goals.

Will your kids be crushed by failure? Will it deter them? If so, success will be hard to achieve. Successes often follow a pattern of failure and adjustment. The people who get discouraged during the process and fail to persevere are the ones who struggle the most to find success. When your kids fail, remind them they’re not finished. Failure doesn’t have to be their final chapter.

Sound off: Do you know how to define success to children? What would you say?

The post Benjamin Watson: 6 Ways to Help Your Kids Define Success appeared first on All Pro Dad.

items.title: 5 Strategies for Parenting an Anxious Teen
items.description:
Is your teen anxious? The answer is more than likely “yes.” More than one in three teenagers in America has been diagnosed with an anxiety disorder. Additionally, the typical teen anxiety around fitting in, making decisions about the future, and learning who they are makes being a teen pretty tough! So what’s a dad to [...]

The post 5 Strategies for Parenting an Anxious Teen appeared first on All Pro Dad.
items.content:
Is your teen anxious? The answer is more than likely “yes.” More than one in three teenagers in America has been diagnosed with an anxiety disorder. Additionally, the typical teen anxiety around fitting in, making decisions about the future, and learning who they are makes being a teen pretty tough!

So what’s a dad to do? Well, there are lots of strategies for helping teens thrive and survive to become functional adults. In fact, you can get some great ideas here! But what about specific strategies to help with anxiety? How do we support an anxious teen so he or she doesn’t just survive, but actually thrives in a season when there is so much to be anxious about? Here are 5 strategies for parenting an anxious teen.

1. Be present.

Nothing creates stability in your teen’s world like you do. Friends come and go. Teachers and coaches change. Culture and technology are evolving rapidly. Your teen needs to have something she can depend on. The challenge, of course, is that a natural part of her development will also have her pushing against you. But don’t take the bait. Your teen’s job is to push you away, but your job is to stay put. Give her space, but remain present. Check in after school, require her to eat dinner with you, grab a few minutes before bed, be around to help with homework, and show up to her activities. It can be difficult to know how to raise a teenager who struggles with anxiety, but start with being present.

2. Set boundaries.

Your teen will push boundaries. This is natural, even good. She’s learning who she is and what she values. She’s testing the world to see how it works. But that doesn’t change the fact that she needs boundaries. Set them for her. She’ll probably hate it, but she also needs it. When everything is an option, it can heighten anxiety, especially for our teens. Give her clarity around your expectations and stick with them. Reasonable, age-appropriate boundaries for teens create order in an otherwise chaotic world.

3. Get advice.

In case you weren’t aware, you don’t know everything. You may know a lot, but there will most certainly be times when you’re trying to figure out how to raise a teenager struggling with anxiety, and you will not know what to do. When this happens, be humble enough to ask for help. Brainstorm with your wife. Call your dad. Process with a trusted friend. Don’t be so arrogant as to assume you can just figure it out on your own. There’s no shame in asking for help, but there is something to be said about being too prideful to ask at all.

4. Get her outside.

I know she loves hanging out on her phone in her room or watching the latest streaming series in the living room. But she was not made to be a cave dweller. She was made to thrive outside. According to the Cleveland Clinic, being in nature is associated with a whole host of positive mental and physical benefits. So look for ways to encourage outdoor activities.

Take a walk together. When you vacation, look for opportunities to get in nature that promote awe and wonder. The world you live in was designed to help with anxiety. You don’t have to look much farther than outside your front door.

5. Pray with them.

If your teen is worried about something, try praying with them. It can reduce anxiety in as little as five minutes, according to the University of Maryland School of Medicine. It also teaches your teen a good way to cope with the stressors of the world, while reminding them that they don’t have to handle their anxiety alone. If you want to raise a teenager who can cope with stress and anxiety better, teach them how to pray by setting aside some time each day—maybe before bed—and praying out loud together.

Sound off: What strategies have been most helpful for you in raising a teenager who struggles with anxiety?

items.title: Kurt Warner: 5 Small Moments That Make Great Dads
items.description:
People know me as the Super Bowl MVP and Hall of Fame quarterback. They probably don’t know that I struggled to get on the field in college. I had a good arm and was passionate about games, but the coaches told me the reason I wasn’t seeing much of the field was that I wasn’t [...]

The post Kurt Warner: 5 Small Moments That Make Great Dads appeared first on All Pro Dad.
items.content:
People know me as the Super Bowl MVP and Hall of Fame quarterback. They probably don’t know that I struggled to get on the field in college. I had a good arm and was passionate about games, but the coaches told me the reason I wasn’t seeing much of the field was that I wasn’t working hard during practice. At first, it made me angry. Who cared about practice? Then it hit me—most of my time in shoulder pads was spent at practice. I was so focused on the games that I was neglecting the moments that prepared me for them. I’ve never forgotten that lesson.

I’m retired from football now, but not much has changed. Most of fatherhood feels like ordinary reps. Most dads try hard to show up for “big” moments like prom, recitals, and graduations. But 95% of your time as a dad will be “practice” moments. You’ll spend it around the dinner table, driving carpool, or losing in UNO. Your kids know you’ll be there for the big stuff, but they want a dad who is a great practice player too. Here are 5 small moments that make great dads.

1. When You Give Your Kids Attention

When I was in the NFL, my time was a precious resource. I would spend hours at the facility during the day working out and then study game tape at home many nights. Being a pro quarterback demanded a lot from me, but my kids wanted time with me too. So, I’d try to strike a fair balance. When people hear “balance,” they think “even,” but that’s not how I see it. I define balance as giving a kid what they need. I gave them full effort and my undivided attention for as long as I could. That meant no game plans at the dinner table. It meant I’d step away from studying to play with them. My kids knew when it was their time, Dad was all in. I’d put off work because giving them half of me was the same as not being there at all. You don’t have to spend 10 hours per day with your kids to be a good dad, but you do have to give them your full attention when you can. Make time for them and put away distractions.

2. When You Give Your Kids Advice

Three of my kids like football. That was easy for us to talk about. The other four couldn’t care less about football, so giving them advice on their hobbies was a little harder. But I learned that kids don’t need you to be an expert. They need you to be engaged. When you pay attention to what matters to them, you’ll naturally find moments to guide them. I may not know everything about horseback riding or theater or whatever they’re into, but I do know what it means to work hard. I’ve had to handle disappointment. I’ve had to keep showing up when it’s hard. So, if I keep showing up for them, I’ll be perfectly positioned to lend practical advice when they need it. You can do the same. Don’t fall for the trap that only experts have something useful to say.

3. When You Choose to Listen

My kids range from age 20 to 37, so conversations are constantly changing. Some are married. Some are in college. Every conversation looks different. But I try not to do most of the talking. Dads make kids feel heard when they don’t turn every moment into a coaching session. I’ve had to bite my tongue over the years when all they really wanted was for me to sit with them in it, not fix anything. Parenting is hard. Your kids need to know they can bring their hurt, joy, and confusion to you, and you’ll pause and pay attention. Listening before you lecture is how to be a great dad.

4. When You Choose to Learn

I know a ton about throwing a slant and reading defenses. I don’t know much about the equestrian world. At least I didn’t, until one of my twins got interested in riding horses. I watched her interact with these giant animals, and I asked a ton of questions. She got so good that she qualified for the Junior Olympics, which gave me the chance to cheer for her. When you learn about what matters to your kids, they learn that they matter to you. There’s no greater gift than that.

5. When You Tell Them You Love Them

My wife and I knew we weren’t going to be perfect parents, but we were sure going to try. I would constantly ask myself, “Did I do enough?” I wanted to know how to be a great dad, and as I grew, I realized what mattered more than helping with homework was making sure my kids knew, without a doubt, that I loved them. They should never question that. Dads make this happen when we show up consistently, put the kids’ needs above our own, and make sure they feel like Dad is a safe place. We are all going to make mistakes. But if we can remind our kids day after day that we love them more than anything else, we build a bond that outlasts our mistakes.

Sound off: What “practice moments” have you been missing?
